Nest.et: From Middle High German nest, from Old High German nest, from Proto-West Germanic *nest, from Proto-Germanic *nestą, from Proto-Indo-European *nisdós.

Nessel.et: From Middle High German neȥȥel, neȥȥele, from Old High German neȥȥila, from Proto-West Germanic *natilā, from Proto-Germanic *natǭ (“nettle”), of unknown origin. Cognate with English nettle, Dutch netel.
Semantic extension of the "nettle" sense of Etymology 1, as muslin fabric was originally made from nettle-fiber yarn.

s: Nestorian (related to Nestorianism or the Nestorian church)
Nestorian (a member of the Nestorian church)
female Nestorian (a member of the Nestorian church)
nestling (small, young bird that is still confined to the nest)

nesteln.et: From Old High German nesteln. Cognate with Middle Low German nestelen (“to fiddle, lace”). Ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *nastilu and very distantly related to English lanyard.

s: the lastborn of a family’s children, especially when pampered (as goes the cliché)
Nesthäkchen.et: From earlier Nesthöckelchen, from Nesthocker, from Nest (“nest”) + hocken (“to sit, squat”) + -er. In the contemporary form reanalysable as Nest + Häkchen (“little hook”).

s: homebird (one who lives with their parents beyond the usual age)
cnidocyte, nematocyst, cnidoblast (a capsule, in certain cnidarians, containing a barbed, threadlike tube that delivers a paralyzing sting)

person who denigrates their own family or country
